articles.author: Puneet-Kumar2010
articles.description:
⚡ From Concept to Console: 
The Birth of ascii-vibes
You want to print text in style… you search for libraries… you find figlet or chalk… but they’re either too heavy, outdated, or just not flexible enough.
I laughed at first. Then I sighed. Then I thought:
👉 If existing tools can’t give me full control, why not build one myself — from scratch, zero dependencies, fully hackable?
🌌 The Rabbit Hole


I dove in headfirst.
5×5 font grids. Emoji mappings. Node.js quirks. Endless tests in the terminal.
At one point I even said to myself:
"Screw it, I’ll make a fully programmatic banner generator if I have to."
Out of that persistence, ascii-vibes was born.
Not a corporate-level package.
But mine.
ASCII banners, emoji banners, inline uppercase, CLI + API — all fully functional.
The first time my banner printed correctly in the console —
it wasn’t just code running.
It was me proving I could build something useful, fun, and fully my own.
ascii-vibes isn’t the end. It’s the beginning.
🖼️ More fonts and emoji modes coming.
I don’t want ascii-vibes to be “just another npm package.”
I want it to be a reminder that a 15-year-old in his room can create something that’s polished, functional, and fun.
People think meaningful packages require millions of downloads or corporate backing.
Here’s the truth:
Code + creativity + persistence = impact.
ascii-vibes is proof of that.
Proof that even if existing tools fall short, you can build your own solution and share it with the world.
💡 So, tell me — if you built your own npm module, what would you create?
npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/ascii-vibes
Github: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/ascii-vibes
articles.title: 🚀 Building ascii-vibes: My Journey to Creating My Own ASCII & Emoji Banner Module

articles.author: Sohan Ram
articles.description:
I have a React app deployed on AWS S3 + CloudFront.
One of my routes uses a dynamic import (import()), and the corresponding JS chunk is very small (~3.7 KB).
On the first load, the request for this file takes about 650 ms, but if I refresh the page immediately afterward, it only takes about 45 ms.
Here’s the request and response details from Chrome DevTools for the file:
Request URL: https://admin.simprosysapis.com/assets/RolesList-DVgRFD0k.js
Request Method: GET
Status Code: 200 OK
Remote Address: 18.66.57.77:443
Referrer Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

cache-control: max-age=3600, must-revalidate
content-encoding: br
content-type: text/javascript
server: SimprosysAPI
via: 1.1 ...cloudfront.net (CloudFront)
x-cache: Miss from cloudfront

accept-encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd
cache-control: no-cache
pragma: no-cache
user-agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7) ...

Why does a 3.7 KB file take ~650 ms to load the first time?
Is this mostly TLS/handshake + CloudFront latency rather than file size?
Is the x-cache: Miss from cloudfront header responsible?
Why does it become so much faster (~45 ms) on refresh?
Is the browser using disk/memory cache or a CloudFront cached copy?
Is there a way to improve the first load time for these small dynamic chunks (e.g., preloading, prefetching, or CloudFront settings)?
Checked headers: content-encoding: br confirms compression is working.
Cache headers look reasonable (max-age=3600).
Behavior is consistent across multiple builds.
I want to understand if this latency difference is normal for CloudFront + S3 dynamic imports, and whether I can optimize the first-load latency further.
articles.title: Why React dynamic import file (~3.7 KB) take 650 ms on first load but only 45 ms on refresh with AWS S3 + CloudFront?
